title: Stiffness has a geometry: a slow curve inside a fast-contracting sheet, drawn two ways
summary: These figures use the classic ROBER test problem to show what stiffness looks like: a trajectory that hugs a slow manifold, a step size set by the fast clock and not by the accuracy needed, a conservation law that can be kept exactly or only approximately, and a resolvent surface that shows the eigenvalues. Companion static figures add the eigenvector-conditioning surface along the ROBER orbit and the RK45 against BDF step counts and step-size traces.

media.alt: Two 3D plots side by side of one trajectory on a triangular simplex whose three axes are fractions of species A, B and C. On the left the true geometry with grey simplex edges; on the right the same path with the y2 axis stretched by a factor of 100000 so that a thin curved slow manifold becomes visible. Colour runs from dark to bright with the logarithm of time.

read_the_figure.question: What is the slow curve that the solution follows, and what does it cost an explicit solver to follow it?
read_the_figure.axes: y1, y2, y3 are concentrations of three species (A, B, C) that sum to 1. The left plot is to scale; the right plot stretches y2 by 1e5. Colour is log10 of time, from the black star (t = 0) to the square (t = 1e11).
look_at: In the true geometry the path is a straight-looking line along the simplex edge. y2 stays tiny, about 4e-5 at most, so it cannot be seen without stretching.

In the stretched plot the path first drops steeply (dark colours, short times) onto a thin curved ridge, the slow manifold (QSSA, the quasi-steady-state), and then creeps along it (bright colours, long times).

Companion stills: the eigenvalue magnitudes of the Jacobian against time (S022); the step size an adaptive solver takes, a stiff toy against a non-stiff twin (S027, 1899 steps against 42); the same constraint kept exactly (hard) or approximately (soft) with drift on a log axis (S022 hard against soft); and the resolvent surface at the eigenvalues (S027).
In the drift plot the blue (hard) curve sits near 1e-16, the orange (soft) curve climbs to order one.

Companion figures. Eigenvector-conditioning surface: the ROBER trajectory drawn over the surface of log10 of the eigenvector condition number against y1 and log10 y2; the orbit runs over a ridge of high conditioning.

Step counts: accepted steps for RK45 (about 7000, almost independent of tolerance) and BDF (from about 40 to about 450 as the tolerance tightens from 1e-3 to 1e-10); the dotted line is the stability prediction for RK45. The second panel plots step size against time with the RK4 and RK45 stability limits (2.785 and 3.307 divided by the fastest rate) below which RK45's steps sit once the transient is over.
read_the_figure.proves: Stiffness shows up as a separation of clocks: the fast direction collapses at once, then the solution moves on a slow curve at a speed set by the slow eigenvalue. A solver that is not stable on the fast clock must take small steps even though the solution is smooth, which is what the step-size and step-count figures count.
if_wrong: A path that leaves the plane y1 + y2 + y3 = 1: conservation is lost (the soft-constraint drift plot).
Step sizes pinned near a constant while the solution is smooth: the solver is stability-limited, not accuracy-limited.

A spread of eigenvalue magnitudes of many decades in the eigenvalue-versus-time plot: stiff. A near-singular eigenvector matrix (here kappa_V = 3.8e4 on the title) warns that eigenvalues alone mislead.
A resolvent surface that is flat around an eigenvalue instead of funnel-shaped: the matrix is far from normal.
must_check: That an axis stretch is stated (here y2 x 1e5) and the true-scale view is shown next to it.
That time is colour-coded on a log scale, because the dynamics span about 17 decades.
That the conservation residual is plotted on a log axis for each method.
That step counts and wall times are given for the stiff problem and a non-stiff comparison.

terms.meaning: A problem whose fastest decaying mode forces an explicit solver to take steps far smaller than the smooth solution would need.
Robertson's three-species chemical kinetics test, a standard stiff problem with rate constants spanning about 9 decades.
The thin curve (or sheet) toward which all fast transients collapse; also called the quasi-steady-state curve.
A combination of states that does not change; here the sum of the three fractions equals one.
Largest to smallest decay rate in magnitude.
The surface of the smallest singular value of zI - J. Funnels sit at eigenvalues; wide, shallow funnels mean non-normality.

remember: Stiff: the solution is smooth, yet the explicit step size is limited by stability of the fastest mode.
A conservation law is a left null vector of the Jacobian: one eigenvalue equals zero.
Hard constraints (built into the structure of the right-hand side) conserve to round-off; soft constraints (penalties) drift.
Plot stiff trajectories with log-time colouring and stretch the thin axis, labelled.
The eigenvalues of the Jacobian at a frozen time describe the local clocks.

steps.title: The ROBER equations
steps.note: Standard published form. The three rate constants differ by nine decades, which is where the separation of time scales comes from.

steps.title: Why the sum is conserved
steps.note: Writing the field as a stoichiometric matrix S times a rate vector r makes the zero column sums explicit. Any method that evaluates S r keeps the sum to round-off; a penalty term does not.

steps.title: Fast and slow clocks from the Jacobian
steps.note: After a time of order 1/|lambda_f| the fast mode is gone and only the slow mode and the conserved mode remain. That is the slow manifold the colour gradient follows.

steps.title: Explicit step limit
steps.note: The step is capped by the fast clock for the whole run, whatever accuracy is needed. In the step-size figure the stiff toy needs 1899 steps where its non-stiff twin needs 42.

steps.title: Resolvent surface
steps.note: The surface dips to zero at each eigenvalue (the dark spikes). For a normal matrix the funnel is a cone of slope 1; shallow wide funnels mean a small perturbation can move the eigenvalue a long way.

steps.title: The stability prediction for RK45
steps.note: The step is held at about 3.3 over the fast rate, so the count is the integral of the fast rate divided by 3.3 and does not depend on the tolerance, which is exactly the flat orange line.

worked.title: How many RK4 steps does a fast eigenvalue force?
worked.problem: A fast decay rate of |lambda_f| = 1e4 per unit time must be integrated to t = 10 with RK4 (real-axis limit 2.78). Minimum number of steps for stability?
worked.answer: About 36 000 steps, whatever accuracy the slow solution needs; an implicit method has no such limit.

analyze.q: In the stretched plot the path is a thin curve; in the true-scale plot it is a line. Which statement is true: the stretch changes the dynamics, or only the picture?
analyze.hint: Think about what is multiplied by 1e5.

analyze.q: The soft-constraint drift reaches order one. What would you inspect in the training objective to explain that, assuming a penalty weight of 1e-4?
analyze.hint: A penalty only trades off against other terms.

analyze.q: The resolvent surface has two deep funnels at the eigenvalues and a third eigenvalue at zero. Where is the third and why is it there?

evaluate.q: A reader sees only the true-scale plot. What claim about the solution would they get wrong?
Is a smaller step count always a better solver on this problem?
evaluate.hint: Cost per step and accuracy on the slow manifold.

create: Re-plot the ROBER solution on a log time axis in three panels, one per species, and say which colour or line style marks the conservation residual.
Design a pair of 3D views for a different stiff problem that stretches the thin direction and shows the true scale in the same figure.

checks.q: What is the slow manifold, in one sentence?
checks.hint: What happens after the fast transient.
checks.answer: The thin curve toward which all trajectories collapse once the fastest decaying mode has died out; afterwards motion is slow along it.

checks.q: Fast rate 2e3 per unit time. Maximum explicit Euler step?
Why does the step size of the stiff toy stay at a roughly constant small value even while the solution is smooth?
checks.hint: Which constraint binds, accuracy or stability?
checks.answer: Stability of the explicit method on the fast mode binds, not accuracy: the step is capped by a multiple of 1/|lambda_f| however smooth the solution is.

checks.q: A soft penalty keeps the sum within 1e-4 at the start. Is that acceptable for a long rollout?
checks.answer: No: the drift in the figure grows over time to order one. A hard constraint stays near round-off for all times.

checks.q: How would you build a hard constraint into a learned right-hand side for species fractions?
checks.answer: Write the field as S times a learned rate vector with columns of S summing to zero (or project the output onto the zero-sum subspace); the sum is then conserved by construction.
